analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fracking loophole in federal drinking-water law and forces drillers to disclose the chemicals they inject underground.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 9, 2013, sent to its Environment and the Economy subcommittee the next day, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Frack Act would have closed the "Halliburton loophole" — a line in the Safe Drinking Water Act that exempts hydraulic fracturing from the rules governing underground injection of fluids. Drillers would have had to file the list of chemicals they pump into each well, both before drilling and within 30 days after, and states or the EPA would have to post those lists on a public website. If a doctor needed to know a proprietary chemical to treat someone in an emergency, the company would have to hand it over immediately. The bill was introduced by Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado with Rep. Chris Gibson, a New York Republican, and 59 members signed on in support — but it never got a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking sites and drink well water or rely on nearby groundwater would gain the right to see which chemicals are being injected underground next to their homes, before and after each drilling job. Doctors and nurses treating suspected exposure cases could get the exact chemical identity on request during a medical emergency, even without paperwork. State regulators and the EPA would gain authority to regulate fracking injection under the same Safe Drinking Water Act rules that already apply to other kinds of underground injection.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents and water users near fracking sites

how_it_helps.text: It ends the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption that lets fracking inject fluids underground without the restrictions that apply to every other kind of underground injection, bringing the practice under federal drinking-water protection.

It requires operators to file, before drilling starts and again within 30 days after finishing, the full list of chemicals injected — including chemical constituents, CAS numbers, safety data sheets, and volumes — for each well.
It orders states or the EPA to post those chemical disclosures on a public website, so residents near well sites can see what is going into the ground.

If a medical emergency requires knowing a proprietary formula, operators must immediately give the chemical identity to the state, the EPA, or the treating doctor or nurse, even without a confidentiality agreement in place.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas drillers and their chemical suppliers would bear the cost: federal permitting and oversight of fracking under the Safe Drinking Water Act, paperwork to catalog and report every chemical by name, quantity, and CAS number for each well, and reduced ability to shield formulas as trade secrets from regulators and doctors. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and chemical suppliers

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves trade-secret protection: companies would not have to publish proprietary chemical formulas to the public, only disclose them to regulators and, in an emergency, to treating doctors.

Repealing the exemption would subject hundreds of thousands of existing and future fracking operations to federal underground injection permitting, which the oil and gas industry argues would add cost and delay to drilling and could raise energy prices; states that already run disclosure registries would operate under a parallel federal regime.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful: people living near fracking sites would learn what is being injected into the ground near their water, and doctors could get chemical identities in an emergency without waiting for company paperwork. The main costs fall on drillers and their chemical suppliers, who would face new paperwork, potential federal permitting under the Safe Drinking Water Act, and pressure on trade-secret formulas they treat as competitive assets. Industry argues the bill duplicates state disclosure rules and could slow a drilling boom that lowered energy prices; public-health and environmental advocates argue that cost is small next to the risk of unmonitored contamination of drinking water. The bill included a compromise for industry — it did not require public release of proprietary formulas, only disclosure to regulators — which makes the refusal to give it a hearing harder to justify on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and to its environment subcommittee the next day, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 1921 was introduced on May 9, 2013, with a Republican original cosponsor, Rep. Chris Gibson of New York, giving it a bipartisan start.
On May 9, 2013 it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on May 10 it was referred to that committee's Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy.
The action history records no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 113th Congress.
The bill was one of a series of FRAC Act versions introduced in multiple Congresses; like its predecessors, it never advanced out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drillers and their chemical suppliers, who keep the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption and are not required to disclose fracking chemicals to federal regulators; residents near well sites remain unable to learn what is injected underground.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers and chemical suppliers

sides.party_line_note: Support was 59 cosponsors — 58 Democrats and just 1 Republican, Rep. Chris Gibson of New York — and the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas drilling and fracking companies
industries.note: The bill repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption that has let fracking escape federal underground injection controls since 2005, and forces disclosure of the chemicals pumped into each well. Companies would face federal permitting, public chemical registries, and pressure on trade-secret formulas they currently guard.

Suppliers of fracking fluids would have to disclose chemical constituents, CAS numbers, and volumes for every injection, limiting their ability to keep formulas secret from competitors, regulators, and affected residents.
